Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad you’re here.  
Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a brief, 10-item screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Anything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and there are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to support you.

I’ll ask each question about the past seven days. When you’re ready, we can begin.

1. Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… no, not really. My sister sent me one of those silly baby memes yesterday and I just stared at it. I used to laugh at everything—my husband and I would joke all the time—but lately it feels like I’m faking even a smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can smile for a second when the baby does something cute, but it fades fast. Most of the time I feel too tired or heavy inside to find anything truly funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with friends, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I still try, because I know I “should,” but the enjoyment part barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I assume it’s because I ate something “wrong.” If he’s fussy, I’m sure I’m not soothing him the way a “good mom” would. I keep replaying tiny things in my head, convinced I’m messing everything up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly feel this wave of dread—like something awful is about to happen to the baby even though he’s right there, breathing fine. I check the monitor a dozen times a night. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t shake the fear.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes my heart just starts racing out of nowhere—like I’m walking into traffic—when all I’m doing is folding tiny onesies. It doesn’t last long, maybe a few minutes, but it feels so real I have to sit down and remind myself to breathe.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. I’ll be making a bottle and notice the dishes are piled up, laundry is everywhere, and I just freeze. It feels like I’m drowning in stuff that used to be easy. I usually get through it, but it’s like I’m crawling to the finish line every night.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—did I burp him long enough, will he wake up in an hour, am I already failing him? Some nights I watch the clock slide past two, three, four… and when I do nod off, the smallest squeak from the crib jolts me awake again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that pretty much sums up most of the week. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears coming for no real reason. I keep telling myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m lucky—but the sad feeling just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week. Yesterday I started sobbing while folding his socks because they looked so tiny and I felt like I didn’t deserve him. It’s not every day, but when it hits, the tears just come and I can’t stop them for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom he deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≤ 12 mo)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, daily tearfulness  
- Excessive self-blame, guilt (“bad-mother” cognitions)  
- Spontaneous panic symptoms (tachycardia, dread) multiple times/week  
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety regarding infant safety; nocturnal hypervigilance  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia directly linked to ruminative worry  
- Frequent overwhelm, “drowning” sensations with routine tasks

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; no evidence of psychosis or mania.

Safety  
Denies self-harm ideation, intent, or plan (Q10). No current suicidal risk factors identified.

Screening significance  
High score on core postpartum depression items (sad mood, loss of pleasure, guilt, sleep disruption, crying) plus prominent anxiety/panic symptoms suggestive of co-occurring postpartum anxiety disorder. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment and monitoring for safety.
